sections.title: Policy and access to the centre
sections.text:
Our Lyon data is recent, so there is no trend of our own yet; the figures below are for weekdays in August and September 2026. The Métropole's own figures fill the gap: hourly use of the car parks in and around the Presqu'île fell by nearly 20% in just over two years, falling faster from September 2024, during major roadworks, and again after the limited-traffic zone arrived [3].

Lyon restricts car access to its centre directly. Since 21 June 2025 a limited-traffic zone restricts entry to the Presqu'île to authorised users in the mornings, with the boundary drawn to keep the 18 car parks there, nearly 10,000 spaces, reachable [0]. The low-emission zone has barred older cars (Crit'Air 3 and worse) since January 2025, for parking as well as driving [1], and the city planned to charge residents for street parking by vehicle weight, €15 to €45 a month [2]. Prices rose too: hourly car park tariffs were up 31% since 2019 [3].

In 2026 the direction shifted. In a February 2026 survey, two-thirds of residents who had noticed the changes called them negative, and a quarter said they came to the Presqu'île less often [4]. In summer 2026 the new Métropole executive froze the 6% yearly car park price rises its predecessor had voted through to 2032 [6], prices at 13 central car parks were frozen from August [5], and the Métropole proposed limiting the traffic zone to nights and weekends [7].

sections.title: Parking developments
sections.text:
The main operator, LPA, is turning car parks into mobility hubs. It announced a €122 million plan in 2022 to move beyond parking, starting with a doubling of its charge points [11], and by 2025 it reported nearly 400 charge points and 6,700 secure bike spaces alongside its car parks and park-and-ride sites [9]. The renovated Terreaux car park, reopened in September 2025, was the first public car park in Lyon with ticketless entry by number-plate recognition, and has guidance lights over every space, 40 charge points and 537 bike spaces [10]. Indigo extended its Bellecour car park in 2024 with a closed bike park [12].

Demand from outside has recovered: commercial overnight stays in 2024 were back at pre-2020 levels [13], and public transport carried a record 519 million trips [14].

sections.title: Operators, location, price and use
sections.text:
Lyon is close to a single-operator market. LPA, a public-private company run with the Métropole [8][9], runs most of the spaces in our research set. Q-Park, Indigo and Effia have a few sites each, and we do not measure theirs. LPA charges much the same everywhere, typically €3.40 an hour, but its day tickets are expensive, around €50, against €12–40 in the German cities in our set.

Despite the price, Lyon's car parks are among the fullest we measure: LPA's garages average 52% on weekdays. The busiest are near the stations and in the inner districts rather than on the Presqu'île itself: Villette P2 at Part-Dieu (85%), Morand (82%) and Gros Caillou on the Croix-Rousse (80%). The cluster around Part-Dieu station averages 65%. The emptiest are out at Gerland and the Confluence, some of them cheaper, at 2–9%, which is why dearer garages here tend to be the fuller ones: the price follows the location, and the location drives the demand.
